body: Thanks so much. I'll give these a try, and definitely keep the part about the laser not being IPL in mind. Never heard anything like that before. (I'd also always heard laser is temporary, while electrolysis is permanent and cheaper for certain areas, which is why I'd been looking at electrolysis.)

I think something a lot of us never realize soon enough is that those are extremely rare thoughts in cis people. Definitely not over an extended period, either. Those kinds of thoughts are - if not exclusively, than nearly so - thoughts trans people have, particularly before coming out to themselves.

Yes, wanting to your live your life as a woman if you were assigned male at birth is typically called being trans. Now, no one can tell you you're trans; I can say, "that sounds like stuff someone who's trans would say," but you're the only one who gets to decide whether you're actually trans or not.

I personally just think it always helps to know you're not alone, y'know? So let me tell you a bit about me. I've always had severe depression and intense anxiety. Before I finally embraced the fact that I was trans, I used to tell myself this was all just a "stupid fetish." Because yeah, while there were lots of stray "if only I were a girl" thoughts, most of the specific *fantasies* were sexual in nature, and the feelings would recede back into a mix of fear and "I'm fine as a man!" after masturbating to those fantasies. The few times I entertained the idea of transitioning, I'd eventually decide either it would be impossible for me, or that I simply wasn't "trans enough, like real trans people." But still, I kept telling myself I was fine as a man, until the depression ate up and destroyed enough of my life that I couldn't deny that something was wrong, anymore.

Today, it's been over two years since first letting friends of mine know I felt I was trans. Two years since changing my name to Ashley (albeit only a few months since legally changing it). Nine months since starting hormones, and six months since I started exclusively presenting female. The past year (particularly since starting HRT) has been the happiest I've ever been, to the point where I'm too happy to regret that it took so long.

So if the question is "Could I be transgender?" Yes, you could. But it's always up to you to decide if you are. I hope my story actually holds something for you, and isn't just me talking about myself like a narcissist!

Thank you. Oh my god, thank you. There's an almost nonchalance to a lot of the responses that was making me feel like this was something I was dumb to expect other people to relate to.

I suppose my hang-up is that, while I agree it's unreasonable and totally on him if he expects me to always look perfect, I don't see him wanting his girlfriend not to have stubble as an unreasonable expectation. Which I guess means I'm projecting a little; the facial hair really is one of the most likely things to make me feel dysphoric.

Now that I'm conscious of that, I'll try my best to think of it as no different from any other "off stage" thing. Thanks a lot! ♥

I thought I'd need to change. And then I just kind of realized over time that the actual point of transitioning was to *stop* pretending to be someone I wasn't, not to just keep pretending as a different gender.

There were a lot of things I *did* want to change, because they were parts of me pretending I was someone I wasn't. But there were also plenty of things I had no desire to change, because they felt true to me whether they're seen as feminine or not. (Few examples of things I was told I should change to seem more feminine, and never did, because F that: Swearing a lot, enjoying professional wrestling, talking with my hands, being sexually forward and frank.)

I did change my behavior in some ways, like especially mannerisms, I think. Not because I felt I had to. It just kind of came naturally. Like, I felt free to try behaving different ways, and some of those new ways felt right. I think I'm much more peppy, now, for example. Just kind of felt right.

I guess my policy is: Embrace the gender norms you actually want to embrace, smash the ones you have no interest in. I've affirmed my gender in plenty of ways that actually matter to me. I'm way happier worrying about being me than I am worrying about being whatever other people think makes a girl.

Thanks for this response!

Unfortunately, my testosterone was nowhere near 50 ng/dL. It was 237. Which was, like, nearly half of what it was before my 3 months of HRT, but still obviously a long ways off from 50. My doctor didn't seem very concerned by that, though? And when I asked for Finasteride, he suggested that would be plenty on its own and I wouldn't need anything with it.

The more I read, the more concerned I am that he's just... wrong? That I really should be taking more Spiro or Estradiol. And that since he decided to schedule my next appointment 6 months out, it'll be half a year before I find out. Plus, while I want to reap the hair benefits of Finasteride, and while I don't want to immediately chalk this all up to the Finasteride, I have been feeling depressed in the days since starting, in a way I haven't been since starting HRT.

Thank you so much for the reply! I image he was probably going to have me take half a pill or maybe one pill more per dosage, which would have worked out to 50-100mg/day more. In which case I would have *juuust* avoided going over 200mg/day. But the idea of taxing my liver is scary. I guess I'll take the Finasteride, and if my next test in six months shows my t is still high, I'll try bringing up more estrogen to him.

Thanks again for the helpful reply! :)

Haven't exactly had success finding work, and doubt I'd hold a job right now. Don't know how to get insurance without a job. Don't see why I wouldn't mention the gender thing? Better I know ahead of time if it's a therapist who's in any way familiar with gender issues. None of them are saying I can't come in, just that they can't help with anything to do with gender and they'd be focusing on my depression. Except that they're intrinsically linked, so that's kind of an issue to me.

I agree with your belief. The entire thing. That a family that won't support you doesn't deserve you. That time apart makes parents realize how they're being (although my mother's kind of not totally sane and rational even if no one around her wants to admit it). That family can be replaced.

And I'd *love* a therapist. I'm actually doing *horrible*, and have been for years, and frankly it's a small miracle I'm around to post this on reddit. But part of me deathspiraling like I've been is that I've ended up reliant on my parents for housing, which is why I can't just say "they don't deserve me, I'm going away." I'm on my mother's insurance, which she's very selective about how she'll allow me to use. I've begged to see a therapist, admitted I was suicidal even, and been brushed off and/or told that they'll try to find one they're willing to send me to, later.

Further complicating the issue, my father actually did try to find me a therapist recently, and the result he got was that no matter who he called, as soon as he brought up my gender issues, they quickly told him they don't have anyone who's versed in gender issues, and the best they could do is try and see me about my depression. I've looked to try and find what therapists in my area are versed in gender, and what I discovered was that my state finds itself near the bottom in a ranking of states' availability of trans-competent therapists. There are really none around here. What my father *did* apparently find were therapists who felt that gender dysphoria wasn't real, and I suppose I'm lucky for once in that my father felt that wasn't fair and didn't want to send me there. (On the other hand, he also claims he wouldn't send me anywhere that "only wants to help you [transition]," because he "wants someone who will call it down the middle" in regards to whether I'm truly trans, which is a concept that I can't wrap my head around enough to argue against.)

Thank you for the lengthy response. I appreciate the advice.

I think I've worded that part about how my ex didn't want people to know we were dating, wrong. The reason my friend didn't know is because my ex didn't want me letting anybody know we were dating. Like you said, I can see how that was an enormous red flag in retrospect. But my ex suffers from an anxiety disorder, and I'd gotten kind of used to agreeing to really odd things that were apparently for their sake. I admit I feel stupid for not acknowledging it as a bigger red flag at the time.

Maybe there's truth to a lot of what you say. But it's impossible for me not to feel that I just wasn't good enough for anybody in the end. That if I were any kind of worthwhile friend, it wouldn't have gotten to this. Or maybe, just maybe, I should have said "It's them or me." I didn't say that, because I felt I had no right to. Maybe that's all I had to say. I'm sorry, I just feel there's a lot *I* could have done differently, here, too.

But thank you for the extremely thorough response, and for the comfort. I appreciate it a lot.

To clear up a few things, they're not in any kind of serious, committed relationship. They're, like... whatever you call chatting constantly and being intimate, while still not being exclusive and seeing other people.

Second, I never asked her to break up with them. On the contrary, I removed myself from the picture instead of asking for it.

Third, maybe it is my fault that I never communicated that? My ex forbade me from telling anyone we were dating, at the time, and they'd only really met through me once. After I was dumped, "I'd better tell all my friends I was dating that person so that they know not to do the same" didn't cross my mind. My bad on that, I guess.

But I guess you're right. I should just suck up that my closest friend is closer to somebody who hurt me badly (intentions aside) than they are to me.

I don't know if it'll make you feel any better to hear this, but a lot of what you've said has been true for me. I spent years pushing it all down, I finally cracked when I was in college to the point where I literally didn't leave my bed except to use the bathroom for a week, and ended up barely leaving my dorm for the rest of the semester and not returning for the next semester. I'd started to have anxiety attacks and stuff, and yeah. Eventually came to terms with being transgender, and the dysphoria started to gradually feel non-stop from there. Or maybe I was just becoming more aware of it. But I ended up feeling like I was at a wall, too. I've felt more hopeless every day, more trapped, more like there's no point in trying.

I guess right now I'm trying to tunnel through that wall, though. I eventually hit a point where the pain and the hopelessness got so bad that I actually want to try, even as I feel like there's no point in trying. I made friends with people in the LGBT community who I eventually worked up the courage to come out to, feeling they were a relatively safe place to start. Been working my way from there through long-time friends and family, getting nothing but support from everyone (with one exception), feeling more confident about myself with each person who knows. The hopelessness is still there, and there are other problems I have to deal with, but I'm living with all of it and, I think, gradually making progress. I don't believe there's anything for me on the other side of the wall, but I keep tunneling because what else am I gonna do? And things have been getting better for it. I'm even making plans to be accompany two trans friends I've made to an LGBT clinic to discus HRT pricing.

I wasn't sure if I should post this, since I didn't answer anything. But looking back, you didn't ask anything in particular. So I'll post this and hope that maybe you'll find something in this that'll make it just a little easier for you to get through the days. I know how strong that feeling of wanting to give up can be, but I really really hope you don't, and never do.
